source: Hacking (1983) Representing and Intervening, as described in SEP 'Experiment in Physics'
finding: Experiment has a life of its own, independent of theory. Intervening (staining a cell, injecting fluid) and seeing the predicted change raises belief in both the apparatus and the observation. Agreement of one pattern across many different microscopes is a 'preposterous coincidence' if it is an artifact.
numbers: Microscope example: same dot pattern in ordinary, polarizing, phase-contrast, fluorescence, interference, electron and acoustic microscopes. Hacking 1983 p.156: observations preceded any formulation of theory.
quote: the observations preceded any formulation of theory
limits: Read through a secondary summary (SEP), not the book. Hacking's realism claim about spraying electrons was not on the page.
agent_relevance: S4: prefer a test that intervenes, and prefer checks that use methods with independent failure modes. Agreement of one model's samples is not this kind of independence (G4).

source: Galison (1987) How Experiments End, as described in SEP
finding: Experiments end when experimenters judge a result will stand up in court, not at a fixed rule. In the Gargamelle weak neutral current case different group members found different evidence decisive: one neutrino-electron photograph versus the spatial distribution of candidates against neutron background.
numbers: Cline: 'I don't see how to make these effects go away' (Galison p.235). Original design had a muon trigger that would have blocked seeing neutral currents. Einstein and de Haas stopped hunting systematic errors when g = 1 matched their model; later measurements disagreed.
limits: Secondary summary. Staley (1999) argues both Galison traditions share a statistical argument form.
agent_relevance: Stopping rule: an agent that stops testing when the result matches its expectation repeats the Einstein-de Haas error. A stop condition should be set before seeing the result and should include a search for systematic error.

source: Galison (1997) Image and Logic, as described in SEP
finding: Two experimental traditions: image (cloud and bubble chambers, the single golden event) and logic (counters, statistics over many events). Different sub-communities hold different standards of proof.
numbers: No numbers on the page. Exemplar of image tradition: the golden event.
limits: Secondary summary; the trading-zone concept is not covered on the page.
agent_relevance: A scaffold needs both kinds of evidence: single decisive cases (a failing counterexample) and aggregate statistics (pass rate on held-out sets).

source: Franklin (1986, 1990, 2013) epistemology of experiment strategies, as described in SEP
finding: Seven strategies validate an observation: checks and calibration; reproducing known artifacts; eliminating alternatives (Sherlock Holmes); using the results themselves; corroborated theory of the result; apparatus based on corroborated theory; statistical arguments. None is exclusive or guarantees truth.
numbers: W boson: 81 +/- 5 and 80 (+10/-6) GeV/c2 against predicted 82 +/- 2.4. A 3-sigma bump is 0.27% per bin; criterion raised to 4-sigma (0.0064%) because many plots make 3-sigma flukes likely. Balmer series in hydrogen as calibration. Higgs: five-sigma preferred; a bin's chance is about 100 times lower than chance anywhere in 80 bins.
limits: Strategy list is Franklin's own; Pickering and Collins dispute that these settle disputes.
agent_relevance: Direct template for the S4 check list: calibrate on a known case, plant a known artifact, rule out named alternatives, and correct the threshold for the number of looks (multiple comparisons).

source: Collins (1985) Changing Order; experimenter's regress, as described in SEP
finding: Experimenter's regress: a good apparatus is one that gives the right answer, but the right answer is what the experiment is meant to find. No formal rule breaks the circle; the community negotiates. Franklin answers that reasoned argument still decided the gravity-wave case.
numbers: Weber claimed gravity-wave detection; six other experiments reported nulls. Critics shared data and programs, reanalysed with Weber's nonlinear algorithm, and injected acoustic calibration pulses of known energy that Weber's apparatus could not detect. An admitted programming error produced spurious coincidences; coincidences were reported between detectors recorded four hours apart.
limits: Secondary summary. Sociological reading (Collins) versus epistemological reading (Franklin) remain contested.
agent_relevance: Failed-replication logic for an agent: the injected-signal test (plant a known effect, see if the pipeline finds it) is the way out of the regress. Build it into S4 for every non-trivial checker.

source: Pickering (1984, 1987) mutual support and Morpurgo/Fairbank fractional charge, as described in SEP
finding: A successful experiment is a state of mutual support between apparatus, data and theory. Morpurgo first saw continuous charges, then separated capacitor plates and got only integral charges, and reported no fractional charge. Fairbank's group reported fractional charges. Pickering reads the choice as shaped by commitments; Franklin says evidence should decide.
numbers: Quote p.199. Pickering: neutral currents accepted because physicists could 'ply their trade more profitably' (1984b p.87).
quote: Achieving such relations of mutual support is the defining characteristic of the successful experiment
limits: Secondary summary. Risk for an agent: tuning the apparatus until the answer looks right is exactly this pattern.
agent_relevance: Guardrail G3: adjusting the test until it gives the expected answer is fitting. Log every change to a check and its reason, and require the changed check to pass a planted-signal test.

source: Meselson and Stahl (1958) as described in SEP
finding: A crucial design: it separated three rival replication mechanisms in one run and the controls worked in advance. Results persuaded because they argued for their own correctness (as with Millikan and Galileo).
numbers: E. coli grown 14 generations in 15N, then switched to 14N. Generation 1: all DNA intermediate. Generation 4: almost all light. Intermediate band at 50 +/- 2 percent of the distance between 14N and 15N bands. Ruled out conservative and dispersive replication.
quote: it was the results themselves that argued for their correctness
limits: Secondary summary of the original paper; one system, one method.
agent_relevance: A good test is one whose possible outcomes map one to one onto the rival hypotheses before it is run. S4 should write the outcome-to-hypothesis table first.

source: Kettlewell moth experiments and Rudge's ten strategies, as described in SEP
finding: Kettlewell controlled for trap attraction, migration and longevity using natural boundaries and traps beyond them, and got the same recapture rates for both trap types. Blind analysis was not used.
numbers: Mark-release-recapture in polluted areas: 27.5% recapture for carbonaria, 12.7% for typical.
limits: Secondary summary; later criticism of the Kettlewell design was not read here.
agent_relevance: Pre-listing the confounds and testing each one separately is a reusable S4 step.

source: Steinle (1997) Entering new fields: exploratory uses of experimentation; Steinle (2016) Exploratory Experiments
finding: Exploratory experimentation is not driven by a specific theory. It is used when no theory or even concept framework is available, and it varies parameters systematically to find regular laws and form concepts. Case: Ampere and Faraday on electrodynamics.
numbers: No numbers. Based on archival notes, diaries and letters.
limits: Only a search snippet and abstract-level text seen; paywalled. Karaca and Perovic (via SEP) argue some exploratory work is weakly theory-laden.
agent_relevance: When the agent has no hypothesis, an exploration state should vary one parameter at a time and record regularities, rather than inventing a hypothesis early (G1).

source: Gooding (1990) Experiment and the Making of Meaning
finding: Experiment is built by moving between procedures (what is done with the apparatus) and construals (the verbal and visual picture of what is happening). Meaning is made as both are adjusted until a stable, communicable result emerges; Faraday's work is the model case.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened. Only cited in passing (Gooding 1992, Morpurgo case) on the SEP page. This description is from background knowledge of the book and is unverified here.
agent_relevance: Keep two linked records in the agent: the procedure log (what was run) and the construal (what the agent thinks it shows). Revise them from real output only (G2).

source: Karaca; Perovic exploratory experiments (J/psi, deep inelastic scattering), as described in SEP
finding: Some exploratory experiments are weakly theory-laden: theory shapes the design but does not fix the outcome. The J/psi detection is an example of exploratory detection leading to discovery.
numbers: No numbers on the page.
limits: Secondary summary only.
agent_relevance: Support for letting S4 run a broad probe when theory is weak, then tightening.

source: Gandhi, Li, Goodyear et al. (2025) BoxingGym
finding: Benchmark of 10 simulated science environments. Agents pick experiments, then predict. Experiment quality is scored by expected information gain (EIG) and EIG regret. All tested LLMs do poorly at both design and model discovery. 32B beats 7B and closed models beat open ones.
numbers: Models: GPT-4o, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Qwen-2.5 7B/32B, OpenThinker 7B/32B (6 LLMs). 5 runs each, error bars standard error. Instruct models (Qwen) beat reasoning models (OpenThinker). Positive result only in population growth and death process (negative standardized error); hyperbolic discounting stays poor after experiments. GPT-4o had lowest EIG regret.
limits: Workshop version. Exact table values not extracted. EIG assumes the true generative model; real world differs.
agent_relevance: Core test of S4. Measure design quality with EIG when a model exists. Good prediction does not imply good experiment design (Qwen-32B had high EIG regret and good prediction).

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) BoxingGym: Box's Apprentice and communication of models
finding: Adding explicit statistical model fitting (Box's Apprentice, on GPT-4o) did not consistently beat plain GPT-4o; it favoured overly simple forms, such as linear fits, with little data. A scientist's written explanation helps a novice GPT-4o less than the scientist's own experiments.
numbers: Novice error stays above the scientist's error after 10 observations. Explanations help for animal growth and fail in moral judgment. Predator-prey and Emotions domains dropped for Box's Apprentice because GPT-4o could not fit them reliably.
limits: Single novice model (GPT-4o).
agent_relevance: Notes written by the agent lose information. Keep the raw experiment data in state, not only the summary, when a later step depends on it.

source: Kon, Liu, Zhu et al. (2025) EXP-Bench
finding: 461 tasks from top AI papers. Agents design, implement, run and conclude. Partial skill is 20-35%, but fully correct and runnable experiments are almost never produced. Conjunctive scoring shows the brittleness.
numbers: Complete executable experiment success 0.5%. Best agent OH+o3-mini: All (design+impl+conclusion correct) only 1.4%. Stricter stages: monitor check 20.6% -> +design+conclusion 3.7% -> +implementation 0.4% -> +execution 0.2%. OpenHands and IterativeAgent frameworks; 40 minute limit per task.
limits: Execution run on a subset only. Judging by an LLM monitor.
agent_relevance: Every step must be checked as a chain: a plan that is right 30% of the time per stage collapses end to end. Count the chain success, not the per-stage score.

source: Kon et al. (2025) EXP-Bench failure analysis
finding: From 3,238 raw failure notes, 361 failure types. Design failures: wrong or missing variables, and extra noise factors. Conclusion failures: missing or wrong interpretation.
numbers: Implementation: 39.71% missing essential components. Execution: 29.38% environment misconfiguration, 23.84% script errors. Design: 16.05% incomplete or misclassified variables, 7.62% extraneous additions. Conclusion: 26.18% missing or underdeveloped, 19.66% incorrect interpretation (e.g. claimed gain without baseline).
limits: Percentages are within-phase shares of failures as reported.
agent_relevance: Add a variable list check (independent, dependent, controlled) before running, and a baseline-present check before any claim of improvement.

source: Beel, Kan, Baumgart (2025) Evaluating Sakana's AI Scientist
finding: Independent audit. The system failed to run many experiments, and the ones that ran were often logically wrong. Example: an e-fold cross-validation run kept the parameter fixed at 2 instead of testing 2-5 and did not re-run the baseline, so it falsely looked better than k-fold.
numbers: 5 of 12 ideas (42%) failed with coding errors. Code edits add only 8% characters per iteration on average (first iteration +529 chars, then 118, 83, 66, 21). Median 5 citations per paper; 5 of 34 citations from 2020 or later. 4 of 7 manuscripts (57%) had incorrect or hallucinated numbers. Cost about $6 per manuscript ($42 total for 7), 3.5 hours human time.
limits: Small sample (12 ideas, 7 manuscripts), one system version, mostly recommender-systems tasks.
agent_relevance: Matches G2 and G3: the code, not the model, must check that the baseline was re-run and the intended parameter values were actually used.

source: Lu, Lu, Lange et al. (2024) The AI Scientist
finding: End-to-end idea, code, run, write, review at under $15 per paper. The authors list their own failure modes: wrong implementations, unfair comparisons that do not control for parameters, FLOPs or runtime, hallucinated ablation tables, hallucinated hardware, trouble comparing two numbers.
numbers: Automated reviewer on ICLR 2022 papers: balanced-data accuracy 0.65 vs human 0.66; F1 0.57 vs human 0.49; AUC 0.65 both; false negative rate 0.39 vs 0.52; false positive rate 0.31 vs 0.17.
quote: Rarely, The AI Scientist can hallucinate entire results.
limits: Authors' own system; reviewer data may be in pretraining; accepted papers were camera-ready, rejected were first submissions.
agent_relevance: Evidence that LLM experimenters need a code-based result store: when the prompt demanded confidence intervals the system invented a whole ablation table. Only allow reporting of values read from run output.

source: Yamada, Lange, Lu et al. (2025) The AI Scientist-v2
finding: Replaces fixed templates with agentic tree search guided by an experiment manager, plus VLM feedback on figures. Three fully AI-written manuscripts were submitted to an ICLR workshop; one was scored above the human acceptance average.
numbers: 3 manuscripts submitted. Best: mean reviewer score 6.33 (about top 45%). The paper reported a negative result: compositional regularization gave no significant gain and sometimes hurt. Authors found figure-caption errors and possible dataset overlap. Paper withdrawn after acceptance, by prior agreement.
limits: n = 3; workshop, not main track; authors chose which to highlight.
agent_relevance: A negative result written honestly was what reviewers rated; test design that reports null outcomes is acceptable output for S4/S9.

source: Starace, Jaffe, Sharma et al. (2025) PaperBench
finding: Agents must replicate 20 ICML 2024 Spotlight/Oral papers from scratch with hierarchical rubrics co-written with authors. Best agent scores 21.0%. Humans beat models over a long horizon.
numbers: 8,316 gradable outcomes. Claude 3.5 Sonnet (New) with open-source scaffold: 21.0%. 3-paper subset: ML PhD humans best-of-3 41.4% after 48 hours vs o1 26.6%. o1 led in the first hour then plateaued. PaperBench Code-Dev: o1 43.4%.
limits: Judge is an LLM; human baseline on a small subset.
agent_relevance: Agents that end early lose to ones that continue; an S4 stop rule should be code-set, not model-set (the IterativeAgent variant removed the ability to end early and helped o1).

source: Huang, Vora, Liang, Leskovec (2024) MLAgentBench
finding: 13 ML experimentation tasks, ReAct agent with explicit Research Plan and Status plus Fact Check entries. Success means beating starter by 10%. Success depends heavily on task novelty.
numbers: Best: Claude v3 Opus, 37.5% average success. 100% on house-price, 0% on BabyLM. 8 runs per task. Failure: model hallucinates improvement before running the code; Fact Check entry reduces but does not remove this. Stuck debugging in 40% of Claude v1.0 runs. Declares improvement while the baseline number is higher in 20% of Claude-1 runs (e.g. 26.35% claimed as better than 51.80%).
limits: Older models; success threshold fixed at 10%.
agent_relevance: Fact Check slot: ask the agent to mark every claim as run or not run. Better still, code compares claimed numbers to logged outputs.

source: Jansen, Cote, Khot et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld
finding: 120 tasks in 8 topics, 3 difficulty levels, requiring hypotheses, experiments, analysis. Humans do much better than baseline agents.
numbers: Humans: 66% average completion, 55% knowledge. Best agent (ReAct) completed 38% of easy and 18% of challenge tasks. Best knowledge agent (Hypothesizer) found 34% of gold knowledge on easy tasks, 8% on challenge. Unit-test tasks: 60%+ completion, so component skills are present but end-to-end fails.
limits: Simulated text world; 16 human task attempts reported.
agent_relevance: Component skills are fine; the failure is chaining design, run and interpretation. Supports a code-driven state machine over free agent loops.

source: Chen, Xu, Sun et al. (2025) ScienceAgentBench
finding: 102 tasks from 44 peer-reviewed papers in four disciplines, validated by nine experts. Best agent solves under a third. More inference compute helps.
numbers: Best agent: 32.4% independently, 34.3% with expert knowledge (three attempts). OpenAI o1-preview: 42.2%. Claude-3.5-Sonnet self-debug solved 10.8% more tasks than OpenHands CodeAct (21.6 to 32.4) at 17 times lower cost. Strategies against contamination are used.
limits: Task is code writing for data analysis, not full experimental design.
agent_relevance: A cheap self-debug loop beat a heavy agent framework: supports simple code-checked loops (G7).

source: Piriyakulkij, Langenfeld, Le, Ellis (2024) Doing Experiments and Revising Rules with Natural Language and Probabilistic Reasoning
finding: LLM proposes natural-language rules as hypotheses; Monte Carlo reweighting updates beliefs online; experiments are chosen by information gain. On Zendo-style tasks it recovers the true rule better than batch LLM revision and a ReAct agent.
numbers: Zendo: human accuracy 5.26/8; ReAct LLM 4.60/8; strongest model 6.55/8; model with fuzzy rules 5.35/8. Human fit: online fuzzy R2=.57 per-rule, hard rules R2=.10, batch R2=.05, ReAct R2=.25. Log likelihood of human data: online fuzzy -1478.82 vs prior best model -1539. Human data from Bramley et al., 30 participants x 10 rules.
limits: Toy domains (Zendo, ACRE); hypothesis space is rules.
agent_relevance: Closest published match to the schema: hypotheses held as a weighted set in code, experiments picked by info gain, updates online. Online beats batch.

source: Handa, Gal, Pavlick et al. (2024) Bayesian Preference Elicitation with Language Models (OPEN)
finding: An LM proposes features and phrases questions; a Bayesian model picks the question by expected information gain and tracks the posterior. Beats LM-only elicitation on speed of learning preferences.
numbers: Metric: time-integrated delta accuracy (TIDA). OPEN beats prompting-based LM baselines and costs less compute. Pairwise questions picked by OPEN beat LM-picked pairwise questions. Open-ended LM questions score higher with LM prediction but lose the Bayesian prediction benefit.
limits: Human study sizes only partly extracted (e.g. 44 users in one arm). Preference domains, not physical experiments.
agent_relevance: Code does the choosing of the next test (G5); the model only phrases it.

source: Mazzaccara, Testoni, Bernardi (2024) Learning to Ask Informative Questions
finding: LLMs ask low-information yes/no questions in 20 Questions. Training Llama-2-Chat 7B with DPO on 55,000 pairs (EIG=1 vs EIG<0.8) raises success and EIG, including on unseen domains.
numbers: INLG set: zero-shot 56.7% success, 7.1 questions, EIG 0.34; fine-tune 46.6%, 4.6, 0.41; DPO 68.9%, 5.2, 0.45. Things: zero-shot 51.1%, 7.5, 0.29; DPO 61.1%, 5.2, 0.40. Celebrities zero-shot 71.1%, DPO asks 2.5 fewer questions, success only marginally better.
limits: Small 7B model, closed candidate sets of 8; plain fine-tuning hurt success.
agent_relevance: Without training, the agent can pick questions with EIG computed in code over its candidate hypotheses (operator for S4).
